questions.question: What does it mean for a subset $\boldsymbol{E}$ of a space $\boldsymbol{X}$ to be compact?
options: Every finite cover of $\boldsymbol{E}$ has an open subcover.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ has no open covers.
Every open cover of $\boldsymbol{E}$ has a finite subcover.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is always the whole space $\boldsymbol{X}$.
questions.explanation: A subset $E\subseteq X$ is compact when every open cover of $E$ has a finite subcover. The definition quantifies over all open covers, requiring each to admit a finite subcover.
questions.source_support: The definition states that every open cover has a finite subcover.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: The definition is about every open cover (not finite cover) having a finite subcover; a finite cover trivially has itself as a finite subcover.
A compact set has many open covers (e.g., $\{X\}$); having none is impossible.
A compact set need not be the whole space; e.g., $[0,1]$ is compact in $\mathbb{R}$ but $\mathbb{R}\ne[0,1]$.

questions.question: What does 'continuity preserves compactness' mean?

If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is continuous on compact $\boldsymbol{X}$, then $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})$ is compact.
Every image of every set is compact.
Continuity turns every unbounded set into a finite set.
questions.explanation: Continuity preserves compactness: if $f$ is continuous on a compact set $X$, then the image $f(X)$ is compact. The continuous image of a compact set is compact.
questions.source_support: The image of a compact set under a continuous function is compact.

Not every image of every set is compact; e.g., $f(x)=x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ gives $\mathbb{R}$, which is not compact.
Continuity does not turn unbounded sets into finite sets; e.g., $f(x)=x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ gives unbounded $\mathbb{R}$.
